metadata.title: The Doppler Effect Is Not Symmetric
metadata.register: formal, undergrad/grad audience, no casual narration
metadata.branding: none — unbranded, book content only, no channel/logo/handle

beats.narration_text: A siren approaches you, or you run toward a parked siren, at the same speed. Do you hear the same pitch?
beats.new_visual_element: Portrait-only opening question card (title-styled, crimson underline).

beats.narration_text: Consider a siren approaching you at thirty meters per second. Now reverse the situation: the siren is parked, and you run toward it at thirty meters per second. The relative speed is the same in both cases. Do you hear the same pitch shift?
beats.new_visual_element: Split screen with a solid divider. Panel one: a white ambulance with a red stripe and cross drives toward a standing stick-figure listener. Panel two: the same ambulance parked, a stick-figure listener running toward it. Both move at the same on-screen speed. Panel titles: moving source, moving observer.
beats.accumulated_scene_state: two panels, ambulance + listener in each, matching speeds

beats.narration_text: When the source moves, it moves through the air. Each wavefront is emitted from a new position, a little closer to the one before it. Ahead of the source the wavefronts crowd together, so the wavelength in the air is genuinely shorter. Behind it, the wavelength is longer.
beats.new_visual_element: In the moving-source panel, teal circular wavefronts emitted at a fixed interval, each centered where the ambulance was at its emission; they bunch ahead and spread behind. A bracket ahead labeled shorter wavelength and one behind labeled longer wavelength, locked to the ring spacing. A small note: speeds exaggerated.
beats.accumulated_scene_state: moving-source panel with bunched rings and wavelength brackets; observer panel still running

beats.narration_text: When the source is parked, the wavefronts are evenly spaced in every direction, and the wavelength never changes. A listener running toward the source simply meets those unchanged wavefronts more often than a listener standing still. The wavelength is the same. Only the rate of arrival increases.
beats.new_visual_element: In the moving-observer panel, evenly spaced teal rings around the parked ambulance. Two counters of wavefronts met: one for the running listener, one for a grey listener standing still; the running counter climbs faster, from the actual ring crossings.
beats.accumulated_scene_state: both panels emitting rings; observer panel shows two crossing counters

beats.narration_text: Two mechanisms give two different formulas. For a moving source, the observed frequency is f s times v, over v minus v s. For a moving observer, it is f s times v plus v o, over v. With sound at three hundred forty meters per second and a five hundred hertz siren, the first gives about five hundred forty eight hertz, and the second about five hundred forty four.
beats.new_visual_element: Each panel's title is replaced by its formula and result: f_o = f_s v/(v - v_s) = 548 Hz, and f_o = f_s (v + v_o)/v = 544 Hz.
beats.accumulated_scene_state: two running panels, each with its formula and numerical result

beats.narration_text: The difference exists because sound travels through a medium. What matters is motion relative to the air, not only the relative motion of source and listener. A moving source changes the wavelength itself. A moving observer changes only how quickly the waves arrive.
beats.new_visual_element: Summary: THE MEDIUM BREAKS THE SYMMETRY, with the sub-line moving source: shorter wavelength / moving observer: faster arrival.
beats.accumulated_scene_state: final held frame: both panels running, summary
